claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
The alloy's uniform solid-solution state favors plasticity and machinability.
The low hardness and strength arise from rapid dynamic recovery during deformation.
A moderately low stacking-fault energy facilitates dislocation cross-slip in this alloy.
Dynamic recovery prevents substantial dislocation accumulation.
Limited dislocation accumulation restricts work hardening and thereby limits hardness and strength.
Room-temperature deformation permits active dynamic recovery in annealed equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Reducing the deformation temperature to cryogenic conditions is expected to suppress dynamic recovery through reduced atomic mobility.
Room-temperature deformation will produce relatively low dislocation-density buildup and a low strain-hardening rate.
Low-temperature deformation will produce a higher dislocation density than room-temperature deformation.
The increased dislocation accumulation at low temperature will increase work hardening.
Low-temperature deformation will result in higher measured hardness and strength than room-temperature deformation.
The proposed mechanism is limited to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply at moderate strains below approximately 15%.
Failure of low-temperature testing to increase dislocation density, work hardening, and hardness or strength relative to room-temperature testing would falsify the proposed recovery mechanism.
